All estimators in `qte.distributional_did` follow the per-cell approach of
[Callaway & Sant'Anna 2021](#ref-cs-2021): for a treatment group $g$ and a period $t$ they construct
the counterfactual distribution of that cell and compare it to the observed one. We are often
interested in effects above the level of the individual cells. In the `py-qte` package, besides the
cell-level effect estimates, effects by treatment group, by event time and overall effects, all _on
the treated_, are available.

In the following, we demonstrate these aggregations using the `mpdta` dataset, a description of
which can be found [here](index.qmd#the-data) in the context of the Changes-in-Changes (CIC)
estimator.

{{< include _setup-did.qmd >}}

@lst-estimate shows the estimation on which our aggregations are based.

```{python}
#| label: lst-estimate
from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig
from qte.datasets import load_mpdta
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_changes_in_changes_effects

QS = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75]

# Kept deliberately small so the page builds quickly while the documentation is being iterated on.
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=50, seed=42, n_workers=4)

panel = load_mpdta().with_columns(pl.col("first.treat").replace(0, float("inf")).alias("group"))

with timer("changes-in-changes"):
    cic = estimate_changes_in_changes_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

## Aggregation

Aggregating distributional estimates differs from aggregating means. To get from cell-level means to
an aggregation level of choice, it is enough to weight the individual cells by their relative cell
sizes. This is not true for the aggregation of quantiles: a sum of cell-size-weighted quantiles
generally does not correspond to the quantile of the distribution that corresponds to the
aggregation level (for instance, the overall distribution of outcomes under treatment and under no
treatment for the treated group). Thus, one first has to construct the aggregate distribution by
combining the cell-level distributions (on a common grid) with the appropriate weights; the
quantiles of interest are then the quantiles of that aggregate distribution.

## By Treatment Group

One effect per treatment group, averaged over that group's post-treatment periods.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-group
cic.group.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-group
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-Changes, aggregated by treatment group."
show_chart(cic.group.plot(), facet_width=200)
```

## By Time Since Treatment

Effects by event time $e = t - g$; negative event times are placebo cells.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-event-study
cic.event_study.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-event-study
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-Changes by event time."
show_chart(cic.event_study.plot(), facet_width=95)
```

## Overall

A single effect, weighting treatment groups by their number of counties.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-overall
cic.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-overall
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-Changes, overall aggregation."
show_chart(cic.overall.plot())
```
